passages.t: In God's likeness, and in Adam's
passages.happening:
A new section of Genesis begins: “This is the book of the generations of Adam” (verse 1). It starts by looking back. God made human beings “in His own likeness”. He made them male and female, blessed them, and called them “man” (verses 1-2).

Then the list begins. When Adam is 130 years old, he has a son “in his own likeness, after his own image” and names him Seth (verse 3). Adam lives 800 more years and has other sons and daughters (verse 4). “So Adam lived a total of 930 years, and then he died” (verse 5).
passages.hearers:
A family line (a genealogy) mattered a great deal in the ancient world. It showed who belonged to a family, who could inherit, and how a people was tied to its past. For the first hearers, this list tied Noah, and later Abraham and Israel, back to the very first human being.

The words ‘likeness’ and ‘image’ are the words of 1:26. God made Adam in his likeness. Now Adam has a son in his own likeness. The image of God is passed down from parent to child. Every person in the list carries it, and so does every person reading it.

But the image is passed down in a world after the garden. Adam was told he would return to dust (3:19). Now the list says it plainly: ‘and then he died’. The first death in the Bible was a murder. Here is the first death from old age, and it is the death of the first man.

Notice too what is missing. Cain and Abel are not named here. The list follows Seth, the son ‘granted’ in place of Abel (4:25).
passages.later:
Luke traces Jesus' family back through this list and ends it, “the son of Enosh, the son of Seth, the son of Adam, the son of God” (Luke 3:38). Luke sets Jesus in the whole human family, not only in Israel.

Paul looks at the same fact this verse records. “Nevertheless, death reigned from Adam until Moses” (Romans 5:14). And in the next breath he calls Adam “a pattern of the One to come”: Christ, the new head of the human family.

James uses the image of God in this list as a reason to guard our speech. We curse people “who have been made in God’s likeness” (James 3:9). The likeness that runs down Adam's family is a reason to honor every person.
passages.asks: Every name in this list was made in God's likeness. Ask whose dignity you find it hardest to honor, and what it would change to see God's likeness in that person. Then notice that the first man's story ends in four words. Ask what you hope will be said when yours is told.

passages.happening:
The list runs on with a fixed pattern. When a man has lived a certain number of years, he becomes the father of a son. After that he lives more years and has other sons and daughters. Then comes his total age, and the same four words: ‘and then he died’.

Seth lives 912 years. Enosh lives 905. Kenan lives 910. Mahalalel lives 895. Jared lives 962 (verses 6-20). Each has a son, and each dies.
passages.hearers:
The first hearers would feel the drumbeat. Long before the list ends, a listener knows how each entry will close. That is the point. God said that the man would return to the dust (3:19), and here it happens, name after name. However long the life, it ends the same way.

Yet the list is also a list of births. Each man ‘had other sons and daughters’. God's blessing, ‘Be fruitful and multiply’ (1:28), goes on after the garden. Life and death run side by side.

The ages are very long, and the first hearers would know that other peoples told of very long lives before the flood too. A Mesopotamian list of kings, the Sumerian King List, names eight kings before the flood who reigned in all for 241,200 years. Genesis is different in three ways. Its numbers are far smaller. Its men are not kings, only fathers. And every one of them dies.

The numbers do not agree in every ancient copy. In the standard Hebrew text, the ages at which the fathers had their sons add up to 1,656 years from Adam to the flood. The ancient Greek translation often gives a father an extra hundred years before his son is born, so its total is more than 2,200 years. The Samaritan copy of the Torah gives 1,307. The ancient copyists already found these numbers important, and puzzling.
passages.later:
The long lives do not last. After the flood the ages fall. God sets a limit on human life (6:3), and by chapter 11 the ages are in the hundreds, not the nine hundreds. A psalm says our days are seventy years, or eighty for the strong (Psalm 90:10), and it prays, “So teach us to number our days, that we may present a heart of wisdom” (Psalm 90:12).

The New Testament names death as an enemy, not a friend. “The last enemy to be destroyed is death” (1 Corinthians 15:26). And Jesus stands at a grave and says, “I am the resurrection and the life. Whoever believes in Me will live, even though he dies” (John 11:25).

Paul does not tell grieving people not to grieve. He tells them not to “grieve like the rest, who are without hope” (1 Thessalonians 4:13).
passages.hard:
Did people before the flood really live for nine hundred years? Christians who take the Bible with equal seriousness answer in more than one way.

Some take the ages as ordinary years. They point out that the ages fall steadily after the flood, which suggests a real change in human life.

Some read the numbers as symbolic or as a way of honoring ancestors. They note patterns in them: Enoch lives 365 years, the number of days in a year, and Lamech lives 777, a number full of sevens.

Some point to the way ancient lists of this kind were written, like the Sumerian King List with its much larger numbers. On this view Genesis uses a known form for the earliest times, and cuts the numbers down to human size.

Can the list be added up to find the date of creation? In 1650 Archbishop James Ussher used numbers like these to place creation in 4004 BC, a date later printed in the margins of many English Bibles. Others answer that Hebrew family lines sometimes skip generations. For example, Matthew 1:8 goes from Joram straight to Uzziah, passing over three kings named in 2 Kings. The precise ages in Genesis 5 make some readers doubt that it has gaps; others think it may. And the three ancient texts give different totals.

Christians differ, and these notes do not settle it. What the chapter plainly teaches does not hang on the answer: God's blessing goes on from generation to generation, death reigns over every life, and God keeps a line of hope alive.
passages.asks: Read the refrain slowly: ‘and then he died’. Ask what it means for you that your life, too, has an end. That is not meant to frighten you, but to make you wise. Ask what you would do differently this week if you counted your days the way the psalm asks.

passages.happening:
When Enoch is 65, he becomes the father of Methuselah (verse 21). Then the pattern changes. Instead of ‘Enoch lived’, the text says, “Enoch walked with God 300 years and had other sons and daughters” (verse 22). He lives 365 years in all (verse 23).

And instead of ‘and then he died’, the list says something no other entry says: “Enoch walked with God, and then he was no more, because God had taken him away” (verse 24).
passages.hearers:
After six entries that end in death, the change would leap out at a listener. The drumbeat stops. Enoch's life does not end with the four words. It ends with God.

To ‘walk with God’ is a picture of a whole life lived close to God, day after day. It is not one great deed. The same words are used of Noah in the next chapter (6:9). Walking became the Bible's most common picture for how a person lives.

The verb ‘take’ is an ordinary Hebrew word. But the Bible uses it again when the prophet Elijah is taken up to heaven: “the LORD will take your master away from you today” (2 Kings 2:3). The text does not say where Enoch went or how. It says only that his life ended in God's presence, and that he did not go the way of the others.

Enoch is the seventh name from Adam, counting Adam as the first. In Cain's line, the seventh was Lamech, who boasted of killing (4:23-24). In Seth's line, the seventh walks with God. Many readers think the two lines are set side by side on purpose.
passages.later:
Hebrews remembers Enoch among the people of faith: “By faith Enoch was taken up so that he did not see death” (Hebrews 11:5). It adds that “he was commended as one who pleased God,” and then says, “without faith it is impossible to please God” (Hebrews 11:6).

Jude calls him “Enoch, the seventh from Adam” and gives words of warning in his name (Jude 1:14). Those words are almost the same as a line in 1 Enoch, an ancient Jewish book written in the last centuries before Christ and not part of the Bible. Christians have read Jude's use of it in more than one way. Many say that quoting a book is not the same as treating all of it as Scripture, just as Paul quotes Greek poets (Acts 17:28).

The prophet Micah asks what God wants of people and answers, “to act justly, to love mercy, and to walk humbly with your God” (Micah 6:8). Enoch's way of life became a summary of faithful living.
passages.asks: Enoch's whole story is that he walked with God. Ask what one small daily habit would make your life more of a walk with God and less of a race. And in a list full of death, notice the hope: death is not stronger than God. Ask whether you live as if that is true.

passages.t: Methuselah, and a son named for comfort
passages.happening:
Methuselah, Enoch's son, lives 969 years, the longest life in the Bible, “and then he died” (verse 27).

His son Lamech has a son and names him Noah. As he names him he says, “May this one comfort us in the labor and toil of our hands caused by the ground that the LORD has cursed” (verse 29). Lamech lives 777 years in all, and dies (verses 30-31).

The chapter closes when Noah is 500 years old and becomes the father of three sons: Shem, Ham and Japheth (verse 32).
passages.hearers:
Lamech breaks the pattern of the list to speak, and what he says is a prayer of hope. The name Noah sounds like the Hebrew word for rest. Lamech explains it with a related word, ‘comfort’ (nacham). He is tired of the curse on the ground spoken in 3:17. He hopes this boy will bring relief.

There is a painful twist. In the very next chapter, the same Hebrew verb, nacham, is used when the LORD ‘regretted’ that he had made man (6:6). The boy named for comfort will live through God's grief over the world.

Readers have long noticed something in the numbers. Methuselah has Lamech at 187, Lamech has Noah at 182, and the flood comes in Noah's 600th year (7:6). Add them up and you get 969. So by the Hebrew numbers, Methuselah dies in the year of the flood. The text does not say so, but it lets a careful reader see it.

This Lamech, of Seth's line, is not the Lamech of Cain's line in chapter 4. One Lamech sang of revenge. This one longs for comfort.
passages.later:
Lamech's hope is answered in part with Noah. Noah's sacrifice after the flood brings a promise from God: “Never again will I curse the ground because of man” (Genesis 8:21).

But the deeper longing, for rest from the curse, runs through the whole Bible. Jesus says, “Come to Me, all you who are weary and burdened, and I will give you rest” (Matthew 11:28). Paul says creation itself waits to be set free (Romans 8:21). And in the Bible's last chapter, “No longer will there be any curse” (Revelation 22:3).

Peter remembers Noah's day as a time when God waited patiently (1 Peter 3:20). Methuselah's long life can be read the same way: a long time of waiting before judgment came.
passages.hard: A word of care. This chapter is full of death, and some readers come to it grieving. The list does not hurry past death, and you do not have to either. Each ‘and then he died’ was a real loss to a real family. But notice that in the middle of the list stands Enoch, whom God took, and at the end stands a father naming his son in hope. Grief and hope sit side by side in this chapter. If your grief is heavy, please share it with someone you trust: a friend, a pastor, a grief counsellor.
passages.asks: Lamech named his son for the hope he carried. Ask what you are longing to be comforted from: the toil, the weariness, the curse you feel in your own work. Then ask whether you bring that longing to the one who promised rest.
